Pregnant females of the Brown long-eared bat undergo a gestation period lasting 65 days [tg = 65 days] when roosting temperatures are maintained at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], a duration that aligns closely with the slow developmental pace typical of temperate vespertilionids. This comparatively lengthy gestation is thought to reflect the energetic constraints imposed by the species' reliance on gleaning insects from foliage, a foraging mode that yields a relatively low-calorie intake compared to aerial hawking. Neonates emerge weighing a mere 1.7 grams [Wwb = 1.7 grams], a birth mass that underscores the altricial state of the newborn pups and their complete dependence on maternal milk for thermoregulation and growth. The wet weight at birth is strikingly low when contrasted with the ultimate wet weight of adults, which reaches 7.8 grams [Wwi = 7.8 grams], indicating a more than fourfold increase in body mass over the course of development—a pattern typical of vespertilionid bats that invest heavily in post-natal growth rather than in large neonates.

In the same thermal regime of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], the suckling juveniles remain dependent on their mothers for a period of 42 days [tx = 42 days] after birth, marking the time since birth at weaning. This weaning age represents a critical transition during which the growing bat shifts from a diet of milk to one consisting of solid insect prey, a shift that demands the development of sophisticated echolocation and flight skills necessary for hawking and gleaning. The duration of lactation is relatively extended for a bat of this body size, a pattern that may be linked to the slow maturation of the auditory and flight apparatus required for successful nocturnal foraging. During this nursing stage, the pups cling to the roost ceiling while the lactating female departs to hunt, returning periodically to feed them. The pre-weaning juvenile gradually accrues mass, approaching the adult body mass of approximately 7.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 7.8 grams] by the time weaning concludes. This ultimate wet weight, while modest compared to larger chiropterans, is consistent with the species' niche as an agile, low-wing-loading flier specializing in cluttered forest habitats.

Sexual maturity, or the age at puberty, is attained at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] when individuals are kept at a temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], meaning that most young bats born in the summer will not become reproductively active until the following autumn. This delayed onset of pubertal development, spanning a full year, is a relatively lengthy maturational timeline for a small insectivorous mammal and likely reflects the need to accumulate sufficient fat reserves to survive hibernation before investing energy in reproduction. The age at puberty is a critical life-history trait that influences population growth rates, as it determines how quickly a cohort can begin contributing offspring to the next generation. In the wild, this timing ensures that reproductive effort aligns with peak insect abundance in the temperate summer months. Post-pubertal adults, having reached the ultimate wet weight of 7.8 grams [Wwi = 7.8 grams], then enter the breeding population. This body mass, once achieved, is maintained throughout the adult life of the bat.

The reproductive output of Plecotus auritus is characterised by a single litter produced each year [F_R_i = single litter produced each year], with an average of 1.33 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1.33 pups per litter]. This annual output—one litter of approximately 1.33 pups—is consistent with records from other gleaning bat species, where single or twin births are the norm. The relatively modest litter size places considerable pressure on adult survival, as population persistence depends on low juvenile mortality and long adult lifespans to compensate for the low annual recruitment. Reproductive females must balance the energetic costs of gestation and lactation against the need to maintain their own body condition for survival through hibernation. The species thus exemplifies a "slow" life-history strategy within the order Chiroptera, favouring offspring quality and adult longevity over high reproductive rates. Based on the litter size and frequency, the maximum daily reproduction rate reaches approximately 0.0036 pups per day [Ri = approximately 0.0036 pups per day] at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], a low instantaneous rate that underscores the species' conservative reproductive output.

Longevity records for the Brown long-eared bat indicate a maximum lifespan of 30 years [am = 30 years] when the animals are maintained at an ambient temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], such as during winter torpor in cool caves or mine tunnels. This exceptionally long lifespan, unusual for a mammal of such small body mass, is a hallmark of the slow life-history pace that characterises many vespertilionid bats. The ability to live for three decades is intimately linked to the species' capacity for prolonged hibernation, which drastically reduces metabolic expenditure and oxidative damage over the winter months. This trade-off between current reproduction and future survival is a cornerstone of the species' demographic strategy, ensuring that even a small number of offspring per year can sustain the population across generations. Adult survival rates must remain high for this strategy to be evolutionarily viable.
